newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Philippines candidate has economy focus.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Philippines candidate has economy focus.

text.p: Revenue-boosting tax reforms may allow the Philippines to buy back a portion of its foreign debt over the next several years, presidential candidate Senator Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo said.

Asked when the Philippines might consider swapping or buying back its Brady bonds, Arroyo said it could, "when we get the fruits of the comprehensive tax reform program -- probably within the next six years."

The tax package to broaden the tax base, streamline collection and improve enforceability, should be fully implemented this year and revenue benefits should be realized after an "adjustment" period, Arroyo told Reuters.
Most revenue-related issues have been resolved, but some specifics, such as the size of personal exemptions, must still be addressed.
She said comparisons between the Thai baht and the Philippine peso have been overdone.
"Our economy is fundamentally sound enough to be able to survive whatever happens in Thailand," she said.
"Whatever repercussions happen in other markets will only be a ripple and not a tide."
A speculative attack scuttled the baht in May, leading to currency controls in Thailand and opening debate on the vulnerability of the Philippine peso.
Accelerating economic growth, relatively low banking sector involvement in real estate lending and a stronger housing market differentiate the Philippine economy from Thailand's, Arroyo said.
She agreed with the Philippine central bank's opinion that the peso should not be devalued, but she added that she would prefer lower interest rates.
"My personal opinion is that we should have lower interest rates, but I respect (central bank) governor (Gabriel) Singson and I understand his explanation," Arroyo said.
Philippine money market experts on Monday said they expected the 91-day Treasury yield to remain in double digits through the rest of 1997 in an effort to fend off any peso attack.
About 40 of Arroyo's proposed resolutions have become law, including many of the country's core economic reforms.
Arroyo was voted into the Senate in 1992 as a member of the opposition Laban party. She left Laban several months ago, however, to form her own party.
